summary: The identity itself survives the critique that killed both predecessors: incarnationId is minted by the same process that mints flushSeq and is CARRIED in CommitRequest (already shaped to cross a node boundary), so it does not change meaning when M5 separates producer and sequencer -- which is where the lease epoch died -- and it takes no clock input, which is where the segment key died under measurement. Three discriminating tests are writable against M4 exactly as it stands, all T0. But two things the decision leaves unstated ARE vulnerable in precisely that shape: the minting site is named with the wrong process noun and is invisible at the seam the ADR permits M4.10d to stop at; and the CommitDelta attribution is not said to be per-SegmentCommit, which is indistinguishable in M4 (every production delta is single-segment) and wrong from M5's first forwarded multi-pod batch. Both fixes are one clause. Neither implies a split.

findings.title: The minting SITE is the whole decision, and it is named with the wrong process
findings.failure_scenario: The ADR says incarnationId is 'minted once per producer process'. Per glossary.md a producer is 'whatever supplies records -- either a remote client POSTing _bulk ... or producer logic inside a gateway'. The process that mints flushSeq is DefaultIngest (ingest module), i.e. an INGESTER NODE process; podId is its podShortId. In gateway shape the two coincide, so the phrase reads fine; in HTTP shape the producer is a remote client, and 'per producer process' licenses an incarnation minted per connection, per bulk request, or supplied BY the client. Every one of those makes the dedup window reset without the ingester restarting -- replays accepted, duplicates committed -- and a client-supplied value makes idempotency caller-controlled from untrusted input. The ADR then explicitly permits M4.10d to 'state plainly that its coverage stops at the sequencer seam', and the sequencer seam cannot see the minting site at all: it is handed whatever value the request carries.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Move the mint from the DefaultIngest constructor into flushLocked -- `new CommitRequest(podShortId, UUID.randomUUID().toString(), flushSeq++, ...)`. Every sequencer-seam test passes (they construct CommitRequests directly, so the test supplies the incarnation and a replay reuses the same value), IngestCommitPathTest passes as staged (it asserts only podId and flushSeq), and dedup is a total no-op in production: no retry can ever match a stored incarnation. The equivalent surviving mutation on the other side is a sequencer that IGNORES request.incarnationId() and substitutes its own lease epoch -- the rejected alternative, reintroduced -- which no currently-required test constrains either.
findings.remedy: Name the site as the ingester-node process (the DefaultIngest instance's construction, per glossary), not the producer, and state that the value is never accepted from a producer. The discriminating test is writable TODAY at T0 with the seam that already exists: IngestCommitPathTest.java:130's `Recording` sequencer plus IngestCommitPathTest.java:79's fixture -- two DefaultIngest instances sharing podShortId 'pod7' must record two DIFFERENT incarnationIds, and one instance's two flushes must record the SAME one. That single assertion kills both mutations above and costs a few lines in a test that already argues, at line 81-88, that a constant or a swapped argument in this key is 'invisible everywhere else'.

findings.title: CommitDelta 'carries the triple' does not say per-SegmentCommit, and M4 cannot tell
findings.failure_scenario: CommitDelta is `(long sequence, List<SegmentCommit> segments)` (CommitDelta.java:28) and commitAll is the primitive, so one delta can batch segments from SEVERAL pods -- BatchingSequencerTest.java:259 already builds exactly that shape, `commitAll(from("pod0",0), from("pod1",0))`. The ADR pins the Checkpoint shape to the field (`podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq)`) but says only that CommitDelta 'carries the triple'. If the triple attaches to the DELTA rather than to each SegmentCommit, a successor rebuilding the window from the uncheckpointed tail recovers one pod's attribution per delta and silently drops every other pod in the batch -- an empty window for those pods at exactly the moment the ADR says duplicates are likeliest. In M4 this is undetectable in production because nothing constructs a BatchingSequencer outside its own test, so every production delta is single-segment and the two placements are byte-equivalent. It becomes wrong on M5's first forwarded multi-pod batch. That is the same M4-invisible / M5-breaking shape that disqualified the lease epoch, arriving through the format instead of through the key.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Write the triple once, after `sequence`, in both encode paths instead of inside `writeSegment` (CommitDelta.java:167). Round-trip tests pass, both new goldens pass (they pin whatever was written), the single-segment production path is unaffected, and CheckpointWriterContentTest passes because its requests come through `observe(List<CommitRequest>)`, not through a decoded delta. Nothing currently required by M4.10c or M4.10d ever decodes a two-pod delta and asserts BOTH attributions survived.
findings.remedy: One clause: the triple attaches to each SegmentCommit, not to the delta. It also makes the ADR's own 'both paths, or neither' free rather than a discipline -- writeSegment is already 'ONE WRITER FOR BOTH VERSIONS, so the per-segment bytes cannot drift' (CommitDelta.java:162), whereas a per-delta field must be added to the v0 flat layout and the kinded layout separately and CAN drift. Then require in M4.10c one test that encodes a delta batching pod0 and pod1 and asserts both triples decode back.

findings.title: The READ rule is stated; the UPDATE rule on an incarnation change is not
findings.failure_scenario: Today's bookkeeping is `pods.merge(request.podId(), request.flushSeq(), Math::max)` (CheckpointWriter.java, capture()), and the minimal edit under the new shape keeps the max. If the stored seq is carried across an incarnation change -- store (incarnationB, max(47, 0)) after poda restarts -- then poda's SECOND genuine post-restart commit is `1 <= 47` under the SAME incarnation and is refused. That is suppression of a real commit, the ADR's own stated primary harm, reintroduced by the fix for it. The prose defends against it only by the field's name and by 'for the same (podId, incarnationId)'; it never says the window RESETS on a new incarnation and the max is taken only within one.
findings.mutation_that_survives: In the fold and in capture(), take Math::max over flushSeq while overwriting the incarnation. The discriminator M4.10d's notes require -- 'a restarted pod reissuing 0 for a NEW segment, which must be ACCEPTED' (backlog-notes.md:304-307) -- is DEPTH ONE and passes: flushSeq 0 arrives under a new incarnation, the incarnation differs at the moment of comparison, accepted. Only a second post-restart commit exposes it, and nothing requires one.
findings.remedy: Either one sentence in the ADR ('a new incarnationId RESETS lastAppliedFlushSeq; the max is taken only within an incarnation') or one clause in M4.10d's row requiring TWO accepted commits after the restart, not one.

findings.title: 'no clock' is a constraint no M4 test can falsify
findings.failure_scenario: The Decision says 'no clock, no coordination', and the sizing paragraph says '16 bytes as a UUID'. Nothing pins randomness. An incarnation derived from System.currentTimeMillis(), nanoTime or podShortId+startMillis differs per instance in every test JVM and passes everything, then collides across a restart under a frozen or stepped-back clock -- reproducing the exact failure that killed the segment key, which this ADR rejected on a MEASUREMENT of that collision (200/200 frozen, 175/200 on Clock.systemUTC() in the standard fixture).
findings.mutation_that_survives: `this.incarnationId = Long.toHexString(clock.millis())` in the DefaultIngest constructor. Two instances constructed in one test are milliseconds apart, so the two-instance assertion recommended above still passes; production under a frozen RTC mints one incarnation twice and suppresses every post-restart commit. No T0 test can discriminate this from a UUID, so it is a production-review item, not a test one -- which is exactly why the ADR should say 'randomly minted, never derived from a clock' rather than leave 'no clock' as an adjective on the argument.

findings.title: The dead key survives in the surfaces a next session actually reads
findings.failure_scenario: The M4.10b/c/d rows were updated; the note under them was not. backlog-notes.md:282 still instructs 'Refuse a replayed `(podId, flushSeq)` using per-pod `lastAppliedFlushSeq`', and :285 still asserts 'THIS ROW OWNS THE END-TO-END ANCHOR, and it needs NO format change: `Checkpoint.pods` already exists' -- both false under this ADR, and AGENTS.md's protocol is that a session reads the notes for the ONE task it picks. Same for the surfaces non-negotiable 8 makes M4.10c responsible for and its row does not name: FakeSequencer.java:27-29 documents the fake's contract as idempotency on `(podId, flushSeq)`, and Sequencer.java:35/46/88 is the PUBLISHED contract stating the pair. A fake and an interface contract naming a key the ADR just replaced is the drift FakeSequencer's own javadoc says a fake exists to prevent.
findings.mutation_that_survives: None -- this is a documentation-consistency finding, recorded because the anchor test M4.10d owes is written against Sequencer's stated contract, and that contract currently names the wrong key.
findings.remedy: Either correct the two note lines here, or add 'the fakes and Sequencer's contract javadoc move with the format' to M4.10c's row. Not worth a round on its own.

what_i_verified: F1 (segment key collides) is discharged: the segment-key option is rejected in Context on the measurement, and filed separately as M4.46.

F2 (window depth) is discharged and correctly: the ADR now states the comparison explicitly as `flushSeq <= lastAppliedFlushSeq` for the same (podId, incarnationId), and names the commitAll case. The `==` depth-one mutation is killable by the replay-strictly-lower fixture the notes already describe (9 then 4), and `<` by the exact-equal retry -- both already listed in backlog-notes.md:337-341.
F3 (M4.10d instructed on the dead mechanism) is discharged IN THE ROW; it survives in the note, filed as a minor above rather than as a repeat.
F5 (retry unit) is discharged: the ADR states flushLocked re-publishes under a new key and puts the choice -- add a commit-level retry or scope out -- on M4.10d.
The ADR's size claim checks out: CheckpointTest.java:153-170 is `aCheckpointAt1600StreamsStaysNearItsSTATEDSize`, comment '~38 KiB at 1,600 streams', assertion isLessThan(64 * 1024).

The M5 exposure of the IDENTITY is closed: CommitRequest's javadoc already shapes the record for a commit arriving from another node, so an incarnation carried in it does not change meaning when the sequencer moves out of process. The residual M5 exposure is the delta ATTRIBUTION (major #2), not the key.

answers_to_the_launcher.does_it_admit_a_discriminating_test_writ: Yes, three, all T0 and all against fixtures that exist: (1) the minting site -- IngestCommitPathTest.java:130's Recording seam, two DefaultIngest instances sharing podShortId mint different incarnations and one instance's flushes share one; (2) the accept side -- at the sequencer seam, same (podId, flushSeq) with different incarnationIds must BOTH be accepted at distinct offsets, which kills the bare-pair mutation and the epoch-substitution mutation together, provided the fixture does NOT also change leader (the notes already say the discriminator is a restart, not a takeover); (3) the refuse side -- within one incarnation, commitAll(S1,S2) then commit(S1) refused and answered with S1's ORIGINAL offsets, which kills `<`, `==` and skip-and-return-current-offsets.
answers_to_the_launcher.is_the_triple_vulnerable_to_the_critique: The identity is not. The lease epoch died because it belonged to the sequencer and stopped discriminating when the processes split; the incarnation is minted by the same process that mints flushSeq and travels in the request, so the split does not touch it. The segment key died on a measured clock collision; the incarnation takes no clock input. What IS vulnerable is what the ADR leaves unstated: the delta attribution (major #2) is exactly M4-invisible / M5-breaking, and the minting site (major #1) is invisible at the seam the ADR permits M4.10d to stop at. Both are closable with one clause each, which is why this is changes-requested rather than a re-decision.
answers_to_the_launcher.M4_46_scoping: The scoping is right and slightly understated. Right: it is the segment path, independent of M4.10 now that the key is not the segment key, and `put` at SegmentPublisher.java:141 with the 'unique WITHOUT coordination' justification at :136-137 is the defect's own statement. Understated in one respect: the harm is not only that the first segment is lost. The chain still names that key in a SegmentCommit and consumers resolve committed offsets through it, so after the overwrite a reader is served the SECOND incarnation's records at offsets already acknowledged for the first -- wrong records at durable offsets, not a hole. Worth adding, because 'data loss' invites a retention-style fix while the invariant broken is that a committed offset resolves to the records that were committed at it. One caveat the row already half-carries and should keep explicit: 200/200 is a FROZEN clock and 175/200 is an artifact of a fixture whose appends fall inside one millisecond -- the production trigger is a clock that does not advance across the restart (frozen or stepped back), not a 87% rate.
